title: Find Servers That Handled Most Number of Requests
statement:
There are `k` servers with ids `0` to `k - 1`, all idle at the start. Request `i` (0-indexed) shows up at time `arrival[i]` and keeps whichever server takes it busy for `load[i]` time units, so that server is idle again from time `arrival[i] + load[i]` onward. A server works on at most one request at a time, and it may take a new request that arrives exactly when its previous one finishes.

Requests are handed out in arrival order:

- If no server is idle when request `i` arrives, it is discarded and nobody handles it.
- Otherwise start looking at server `i % k` and go up through the ids, wrapping from `k - 1` back to `0`; the first idle server found takes the request.

`arrival` is strictly increasing. Return the ids of every server that handled the largest number of requests, in any order.
signature: List<Integer> busiestServers(int k, int[] arrival, int[] load)
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating directly means, for each request, scanning up to `k` servers from `i % k` to find an idle one: O(n·k). Two questions are really being asked at each request: "which servers have finished by now?" and "what is the first idle id at or after `i % k`, wrapping around?". A min-heap ordered by finish time answers the first, and a sorted set of idle ids answers the second with a binary search.

## Approach

1. `free` is a sorted array of idle server ids (all of them at first), `busy` a min-heap of `[finishTime, server]`, and `handled` counts requests per server.
2. For request `i`, pop every busy entry whose finish time is at most `arrival[i]` and insert its server back into `free` at its sorted position.
3. If `free` is empty, the request is dropped.
4. Otherwise `lowerBound(i % k)` finds the first idle id at or after `i % k`; if there is none, wrap to `free[0]`, the smallest idle id.
5. Remove that server from `free`, count the request, and push `[arrival[i] + load[i], server]` onto `busy`.
6. Return every id whose count equals the maximum.

## Example 1, step by step

`k = 3`, `arrival = [1,2,3,4,5]`, `load = [5,2,3,3,3]`.

- Requests 0, 1, 2 take servers 0, 1, 2 (finishing at 6, 4, 6); `free` becomes empty.
- Request 3 at time 4: server 1 finished at 4, so it returns to `free = [1]`. `i % k = 0`, and `lowerBound(0)` gives server 1, which takes it until 7.
- Request 4 at time 5: nothing has finished, `free` is empty, so it is dropped.
- `handled = [1, 2, 1]`, so the answer is `[1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log k) for the heap operations and binary searches, plus the element shifts of `splice` on an array of at most `k` ids (a balanced tree would make those O(log k) as well).
- Space: O(k) for `free`, `busy` and `handled`.

## Pitfalls

- A server whose request finishes exactly at `arrival[i]` is idle again, so release with `<=`.
- When no idle id is at or after `i % k`, wrap to the smallest idle id instead of dropping the request.
- Release finished servers before checking whether every server is busy.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `free` | sorted ids of idle servers |
| `busy` | min-heap of `[finishTime, server]` for servers at work |
| `handled` | number of requests each server took |
| `pos` | index in `free` of the server chosen for request `i` |
| `most` | the largest count in `handled` |
